newsitem.title: GERMANY: Press says German EMU debate now "Euro-voodoo".
newsitem.headline: Press says German EMU debate now "Euro-voodoo".

text.p: Germany's heated EMU debate has turned into "political ping-pong" with complex rituals that even seasoned observers have trouble following, German newspapers commented on Wednesday.
An apparent truce between Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Euro-sceptic Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber on Tuesday was only the latest act in the long-running drama, they said.

The debate over Maastricht's three percent deficit-to-GDP target has become so entangled that commentators could not say who won the latest round in which Kohl, under heavy pressure from Stoiber, opted for a super-strict interpretation.

But they agreed that hitting the 3.0 percent bulls-eye or landing a few tenths of a percent over it was no longer the main issue, neither for international markets nor for the German domestic political rivalries building up around it.

"Germany's Euro-policy looks more an more like a pagan cult," the popular Munich daily TZ commented. "Voo-doo priest Edmund Stoiber repeats the magic number 3.0 in a trance so often that Chief Helmut Kohl finally falls for its magic."
The politicians could ignore economists' warnings that Germany could not meet the target but should not overlook widespread popular opposition to giving up the deutschemark.
"The voters don't like this Euro magic potion," TZ wrote. "It's becoming clear the criteria debate is meant to cover over the general unwillingness to accept the monetary union."

The respected Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung compared the Kohl-Stoiber debate to "ping-pong with words" and said: "Kohl and Stoiber slam words back and forth with such force that the audience has trouble counting the points."
Kohl's decision to embrace the hardline 3.0 percent target, which Stoiber says Germany must meet or delay the euro's 1999 launch, looked like a win on points for the Bavarian premier.
But by stressing the criterion was "no problem" and that the euro must start on time, Kohl may have outfoxed Stoiber.
"The match is not over," it added. "There will be many more rounds, even if the rival Christian Democrats again change the words that they smash back and forth."
Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung saw Kohl and Stoiber praying the same "Euro-prayer" but with different intentions in mind.
"Stoiber preaches 3.0 percent to destroy the euro and Kohl is now copying him to save it," the city's leading daily wrote.
"Stoiber triumphs and announces that he and Kohl are pulling on the same rope. He's wrong. Kohl is pulling this rope to make a noose out of it for Stoiber."
The Berlin daily Die Welt called the debate "increasingly bizarre" and suspected the bickering over percentage points was meant to spare voters some uncomfortable truths about EMU.
"The question of meeting the deficit target precisely plays no role any more for the markets," Frankfurt's Boersen-Zeitung wrote in a report on a Commerzbank study about the euro.
The bank's index of EMU prospects showed an 86 percent probability it would start on time -- two percentage points up from last week's index, it noted.
